reader.title: Niptown half-way lynching
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A group the paper called 'the boys up at Niptown' hanged an accused thief without killing him, in what the item called a 'half-way lynching party' with a warning of death for a further offense (A1, A2).

The man was hung up 'till he grew black and blue' and was warned that his next offense would bring 'Judge Lynch's death warrant', so he was not killed (A1, A2); the punishment for alleged petty theft was extralegal, but the size of 'the boys' is not given.
All four printings carry one text, which two papers credit to the Cherry Creek News (A4, A5); no independent account was found (A1, A2).

summary.text: The Niptown half-way lynching was the nonfatal hanging of an accused petty thief by a group that a Nevada newspaper item called "the boys up at Niptown," on a Tuesday in late December 1881, probably December 27.
The man was hung up until he was bruised and let live, and the item warned that a further offense would bring his death at the hands of "Judge Lynch."
A brief item about it, credited to the Cherry Creek News, circulated in several Nevada papers in the following weeks.
The man, who is not named and whose race is not given, was described as "a petty larceny thief" accused of helping himself to "several small sums of money belonging to others."
According to the item, a search of his cabin turned up more bar-room spoons than "Butler is credited with getting away with at New Orleans."
On "Tuesday last," "the boys up at Niptown" held what the item called "a half-way lynching party."
The accused was "hung up till he grew black and blue" but was not killed.
The item closed with the warning that "his next offense will be the signal for Judge Lynch's death warrant."
No report of an arrest, an official inquiry or any later act against the man appears in the coverage.
The earliest printing found ran on December 31, 1881, in the White Pine News at Treasure City under the heading "Strung Him Up."
The Eureka Daily Sentinel printed the same words without credit on January 5, 1882, among a run of Cherry Creek local news.
The Silver State at Winnemucca, on January 6, and the Weekly Elko Independent, on January 15, reprinted it with the credit "says the Cherry Creek News."
Every version used the same light tone, treating the man's guilt as settled and presenting the hanging as a warning, without criticism.
None of the printings mentioned race, and none commented on the hanging beyond the original item's joke about the spoons.

accounts.label: Cherry Creek News item (as reprinted)
accounts.gist: The boys at Niptown held a 'half-way lynching party' on Tuesday last, hanging an accused petty thief until he was black and blue; his next offense would bring 'Judge Lynch's death warrant'.

framing.detail: Headed 'Strung Him Up' and told as a joke (the spoons outdoing 'Butler... at New Orleans'), treating the accused as guilty and the hanging as a warning without condemning it.
Reprinted verbatim among local and state briefs, unattributed in Eureka and credited to the Cherry Creek News in Winnemucca and Elko.

record_check.dossier: A Tuesday no later than 1881-12-27 ('Tuesday last' in an item printed 1881-12-31); 1882-01-03 falls after the first printing
4 printings in 4 papers, first 1881-12-31 (White Pine News), last 1882-01-15
Not stated in any printing; nothing in the text shows the man was Black ('black and blue' describes bruising)
Hanging only; no pursuit or seizure is described
A deliberately partial ('half-way') hanging with a threat of death for a further offense; no attempt to kill is described
That id is a store-for-rent advertisement; the item is sn84022044/1882-01-05/p1/a200007

info: 'Tuesday last' before the item ran; the earliest printing is dated Saturday 1881-12-31, so the hanging took place on a Tuesday no later than 1881-12-27, probably that day
one unnamed man described as 'a petty larceny thief'; race not stated
accused of having 'helped himself to several small sums of money belonging to others'; a search of his cabin was said to have found many bar-room spoons
